title: Not a lack of attention: what the ADHD brain regulates differently
hook: Hyperfocus for six hours, but no start on the tax form. The name is misleading: attention is there, the steering is not.

lines.text: The name says attention deficit. So how can someone with ADHD spend six hours on a game or a project and forget to eat?
If attention were simply missing, that would be impossible. It is called hyperfocus, and most people with ADHD know it well.
So the name is misleading. There is not too little attention. There is too little control over where it goes.
Think of a strong spotlight with a loose handle. The light is bright, but it swings to whatever is most exciting.
Today: what exactly the brain regulates differently, and why willpower alone does not fix it.

lines.text: First, the basics. ADHD is common: roughly five to seven of every hundred children, and about two to three of every hundred adults.
And it runs in families. Studies of twins put the heritability at about 74 percent.
For comparison: body height is around 80 percent. So ADHD is inherited almost as strongly as how tall you are.
That rules out the popular explanations. Not bad parenting, not too much sugar, not too many screens.
Those things can make symptoms better or worse. But they do not create the condition.

scenes.title: The management of the brain

lines.text: So what is regulated differently? The key term is executive functions. Think of them as the management of the brain.
They hold a plan in mind while you work. That part is called working memory.
They stop an impulse before you act on it. And they get you started on a task, or make you switch to another one.
These functions sit mainly in the front of the brain, and in its connections to deeper regions.
In ADHD, this management works less reliably. The staff is skilled. But the manager is often out of the office.

lines.text: This management depends on two messenger substances: dopamine and noradrenaline.
Dopamine is often called the happiness chemical. That is wrong. It is closer to a signal that says: this is worth your effort.
Noradrenaline works more like a volume control. It makes the important signal stand out from the background noise.
Nerve cells release these substances into a tiny gap, and then pump them back in. Remember that pump. It comes back later.
In ADHD, this signaling is weaker in exactly the circuits that do the managing.

lines.text: How do we know? In 2009, researchers scanned 53 adults with ADHD who had never taken medication, and 44 adults without ADHD.
In the reward pathway of the ADHD group, they found fewer docking sites for dopamine.
And the lower the values, the stronger the attention problems. A follow-up analysis linked low values to lower motivation as well.
What does that mean in daily life? A task that is important but boring produces a weaker “worth it” signal.
It is not that the person does not care. The brain does not deliver the push that turns caring into starting.

lines.text: A second finding fits right in. For everyone, a reward in the future feels smaller than the same reward now.
With ADHD, this drop is steeper on average. “Later” loses its value faster.
Take a report that is due in three weeks. Today, the deadline has almost no pull. The brain treats it as not real yet.
The night before, everything changes. Urgency supplies the missing signal, and the work suddenly flows.
This is why putting things off and brilliant last-minute work so often appear in the same person.

quiz.q: Mara cares a lot about her thesis but cannot start for three weeks. The night before the deadline, she writes well. Which explanation fits best?

options.text: She simply works better at night than during the day
options.why: A late body clock is common with ADHD, but it cannot explain three weeks without a start. Those weeks had nights too.

options.text: The far deadline gave almost no “worth it” signal. Urgency finally supplied it
options.why: Caring was there all along. What was missing was the push that turns caring into starting, and a close deadline delivers that push.

options.text: She did not really care about the thesis until the end
options.why: The research separates caring from starting. Many people with ADHD care intensely and suffer because they still cannot begin.

quiz.explain: Imagine a car with a weak starter motor. The engine is fine, and the driver wants to leave. But the car only starts when it rolls downhill. A close deadline is that hill. Three weeks before, the road is flat: the reward is far away, and with ADHD a far reward loses its pull especially fast. The night before, the road drops steeply, urgency floods the system, and the engine catches. From outside, it looks like laziness followed by a miracle. Inside, it is one and the same mechanism.

lines.text: So what does switch the system on? Clinicians see the same four things again and again.
Interest, novelty, challenge and urgency. Notice what is missing: importance alone is not on the list.
This also explains hyperfocus. When a task delivers a strong signal by itself, the weak steering fails in the other direction. You cannot pull away.
And it explains a painful misunderstanding. Others say: you can focus when you want to. But wanting is not what decides it.

lines.text: There is a third piece. Your brain has a network that is active when you daydream. It is called the default mode network.
When you start a task, this network normally goes quiet, and the task networks take over.
In ADHD, it goes quiet less reliably. It keeps breaking into the task. That is one well-studied explanation for sudden gaps in attention.
You know the result: you read a whole page, and nothing has arrived.
It also explains the most typical sign of ADHD. Not constant weakness, but performance that swings from day to day.

quiz.q: A student with ADHD scores 95 percent on one test and 55 percent on a very similar one a week later. What does this pattern suggest?

options.text: The ability is there, but access to it is unreliable
options.why: Large swings in performance are one of the most typical signs of ADHD. The 95 shows what the student can do when the steering holds.

options.text: The student did not study for the second test
options.why: That is the usual guess, and often wrong. With ADHD, the same preparation can lead to very different results on different days.

options.text: The good result was luck, and the real level is the lower one
options.why: Nobody reaches 95 percent by luck. The high score proves the knowledge exists. The low one shows it could not be used that day.

quiz.explain: Think of a radio with a loose cable. On some days the music is perfectly clear. On others it cuts out again and again. The station is always broadcasting, and the speakers are fine. The connection is the problem. In ADHD, the daydream network breaks into the task from time to time, and each break costs a piece of the test. So a result measures two things at once: what the student knows, and how well the steering held that day. Judging by the worst day misses the first. Judging by the best day misses the second.

scenes.title: A brain on a later schedule
scenes.svg:
<text x="200" y="36" class="mid ts fm" data-l="0" data-fx="up">scans of 223 children with ADHD, 223 without</text>

<text x="200" y="262" class="mid ts fm">age when the cortex reaches its peak</text>
</g>
<g data-l="1" data-fx="up">
<circle cx="120" cy="210" r="8" class="fm"/><text x="120" y="190" class="mid tm">7.5</text><text x="120" y="170" class="mid ts fm">typical</text>
</g>
<g data-l="1" data-fx="up" data-d="3">
<circle cx="216" cy="210" r="9" class="fc"/><text x="216" y="190" class="mid tl tb fc">10.5</text><text x="216" y="166" class="mid ts fc">ADHD</text>
<g ><line x1="120" y1="126" x2="206" y2="126" class="sb"/><polygon points="216,126 206,131.5 206,120.5" class="fb"/></g>
<text x="168" y="114" class="mid ts fb tb">about 3 years later</text>
</g>
<text x="200" y="300" class="mid ts fa tb" data-l="2" data-fx="up">largest delay: the prefrontal regions</text>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="326" width="352" height="42" rx="12" class="fp"/>
<text x="200" y="353" class="mid tm">a later schedule, not a broken plan</text>
</g>

lines.text: Is the ADHD brain damaged? Brain scans of 223 children with ADHD and 223 without point to something else.
The outer layer of the brain, the cortex, matures in the same order in both groups. But with ADHD, it reaches its peak about three years later.
The delay is largest in the prefrontal regions, exactly where the management sits.
So it is a later schedule, not a broken plan. Many children catch up in part. For a large share, symptoms continue into adult life.

lines.text: The picture most people have of ADHD is a fidgety boy. That picture misses a lot of people.
In adults, the visible restlessness often moves inside. It turns into racing thoughts and a constant feeling of being driven.
And there is a quiet form with hardly any hyperactivity: drifting off, losing things, forgetting appointments.
This quiet form is easy to overlook, especially in girls and women. Many are diagnosed late, or never.

<text x="200" y="52" class="mid tm" data-l="0" data-fx="up">a stimulant that calms?</text>

<text x="200" y="88" class="mid ts fa tb" data-l="2" data-fx="up">more signal stays in the gap</text>
<text x="200" y="108" class="mid ts fm" data-l="3" data-fx="up">a louder conductor, not a sedated orchestra</text>
<g data-l="4" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="346" width="352" height="42" rx="12" class="fp"/>

lines.text: Now a puzzle. The best-studied ADHD medications are stimulants. Why would a stimulant calm a restless person?
Remember the pumps that pull dopamine and noradrenaline back into the cell. The medication partly blocks them.
So more of both substances stays in the gap. The signal in the managing circuits gets stronger.
It does not sedate the orchestra. It gives the conductor a louder voice. Control improves, and calm follows.
A review of 133 controlled trials found clear effects in the short term. Long-term effects are less well studied, and the decision belongs with a doctor.

quiz.q: Why can a stimulant make a person with ADHD calmer instead of more restless?

options.text: People with ADHD react to stimulants in the opposite way to everyone else
options.why: That is a common myth. Studies show that stimulants act in the same direction in people without ADHD. With ADHD, there is simply more to gain.

options.text: It strengthens the signal in the managing circuits, so control improves
options.why: More dopamine and noradrenaline stay in the gap. The management gets a clearer signal, and better control looks like calm from outside.

options.text: It tires the brain, so there is less energy for restlessness
options.why: A stimulant does not tire the brain. It raises activity, but in the circuits that brake and steer.

quiz.explain: Picture a classroom with a substitute teacher whose voice is too quiet. The children are not bad, but nobody is steering, so the room gets loud. Now hand the teacher a microphone. You have added energy to the room, and yet it becomes calmer, because the one who steers can finally be heard. A stimulant works like that microphone. It does not press the children into their seats. It raises the level of the two messenger substances in the steering circuits of the brain, and the calm is a result of better control.

scenes.title: Feelings use the same brakes
scenes.svg:
<text x="200" y="40" class="mid ts fm" data-l="0" data-fx="up">the same brakes, applied to feelings</text>
<g data-l="0" data-fx="up"><path d="M40 120 q20 -24 40 0 t40 0 t40 0 t40 0 t40 0 t40 0 t40 0 t40 0" class="fn sm s3"/><text x="44" y="84" class="ts fm">typical</text></g>
<path d="M40 230 q20 -84 40 0 t40 0 t40 0 t40 0 t40 0 t40 0 t40 0 t40 0" class="fn sc s3" data-l="1" data-fx="draw"/>

<g data-l="2" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="328" width="352" height="42" rx="12" class="fp"/>
<text x="200" y="355" class="mid ts">not a character flaw: the same steering problem</text>
</g>

lines.text: The same management also brakes emotions. So this part is affected too, even though the official criteria do not list it.
Frustration, excitement or hurt arrive faster, hit harder, and are harder to set aside.
Studies find this in a large share of adults with ADHD. It is not a character flaw. It is the same steering problem, applied to feelings.

scenes.title: Knowing is not the problem
scenes.svg:
<text x="200" y="40" class="mid ts fm" data-l="0" data-fx="up">Russell Barkley</text>
<g data-l="1" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="64" width="150" height="62" rx="14" class="fp"/><text x="99" y="92" class="mid ts">knowing</text><text x="99" y="112" class="mid ts">what to do</text>
<path d="M146 78 l6 6 l12 -12" class="fn sd"/>
<rect x="226" y="64" width="150" height="62" rx="14" class="fp sc"/><text x="301" y="92" class="mid ts">doing</text><text x="301" y="112" class="mid ts">what you know</text>
<path d="M178 95 H194 M206 95 H222" class="fn sc"/>
<text x="200" y="156" class="mid ts fc tb">the break is here, not in the knowing</text>
</g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up">
<text x="200" y="210" class="mid tm">“just try harder”</text><path d="M128 205 H272" class="fn sc"/>
<text x="200" y="234" class="mid ts fm">asks the weakest system to fix itself</text>
</g>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up">
<path d="M120 318 h160 v-18 q0 -8 -8 -8 h-20 l-16 -22 h-58 l-16 22 h-34 q-8 0 -8 8 z" class="fn sb"/>
<circle cx="158" cy="320" r="12" class="fk sb"/><circle cx="244" cy="320" r="12" class="fk sb"/>
<text x="200" y="364" class="mid tm fb tb">fast engine, loose steering</text>
<text x="200" y="386" class="mid ts fm">intelligence does not protect</text>

lines.text: Put it all together, and one sentence from the researcher Russell Barkley fits well.
ADHD is not a problem of knowing what to do. It is a problem of doing what you know.
That is why advice like “just try harder” fails. It asks the weakest system to fix itself.
And that is why intelligence does not protect. A fast engine does not help when the steering is loose.

</g>
<g data-l="4" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="296" width="352" height="42" rx="12" class="fp"/>
<text x="200" y="323" class="mid tm">the right tools for this kind of brain</text>

<text x="200" y="372" class="mid ts fm" data-l="4" data-fx="up" data-d="5">next ADHD episode: the bent sense of time</text>

lines.text: What follows from all this? If the inner management is unreliable, move parts of it outside your head.
Make time visible, with a clock or timer you can see. And make the next step visible, written where you will trip over it.
Bring the reward closer. A small payoff right after a step works better than a big one next month.
And borrow urgency or interest on purpose: a deadline with another person, working next to someone, or turning a dull task into a race.
These are not crutches. They are the right tools for this kind of brain. The next ADHD episode shows how ADHD bends the sense of time.

takeaways: ADHD is not too little attention. It is too little control over where attention goes. Hyperfocus is part of the same problem.
It is common and about 74 percent heritable, close to body height. Parenting, sugar or screens do not create it.
The steering system (executive functions) depends on dopamine and noradrenaline, and this signaling is weaker in ADHD.
Rewards in the future lose their pull faster. Interest, novelty, challenge and urgency switch the system on. Importance alone does not.
The daydream network breaks into tasks, which explains gaps in attention and performance that swings from day to day.
It is a problem of doing, not of knowing. So the practical answer is to move the management outside: visible time, visible next steps, near rewards, borrowed urgency.
